chapters.title:
Make the work
disappear.
chapters.lead: A field masterclass in factorization, cached sweeps, Rust, SIMD, and handwritten assembly. Follow one real investigation from an honest reference to a billion-row experiment.
chapters.body:
The fastest instruction is the one
your architecture no longer needs.

We began with a small Rust repository that already knew a powerful trick: an experiment row is not an indivisible unit of computation. We ended with an integrated pipeline, a preserved reference, a complete scaling study, and a Git-backed evidence trail.

This is the whole journey, including the misleading comparisons, the underfilled vector lanes, the hardware changes, and the final handoff. The achievement is not one multiplier. It is learning which work to remove, which work to accelerate, and which claims the measurements can support.

RECORDED RUN · AMD EPYC 9V74
$ TERASWEEP_LEVEL=assembly
… 1000000000 summary.json
98.29s

One billion sampled rows. Complete process.
One measured run. Not one billion independent fits.

Valid rows727,869,685
Cached failed-fit rows272,130,315
Native large-run timingsProjected, not executed
01 / THE LEARNING CONTRACT
UNDERSTAND

Factor the dependency graph.

Separate fixed-data work, model work, signal-path work, and cost work. Share results only when the inputs that determine them are identical.

EXPERIMENT

Choose the right SIMD axis.

Pack independent score jobs into lanes, preserve time order, and see why wider vectors initially failed to improve throughput.

DEFEND

Make the denominator visible.

Distinguish a kernel gain, a complete-process gain, and a native-reference projection. Do not manufacture a cumulative ratio across experiments.

What was inherited, and what was added?

The original Terasweep already contained shared ridge statistics, fitted-prediction reuse, score caching, factored cost arithmetic, and winner-only detail reporting. This investigation added the minimal native Limen Ridge SFD, controlled comparisons, profiling, the constant-signal shortcut, compact cache/scheduling, Rust AVX-512 intrinsics, an authored assembly kernel, validation, scaling experiments, and the evidence handoff.

The route through the investigation

BEFORE THE SESSION

A factorized Rust runner already exists.

The preserved baseline becomes the control, not a blank slate. Other model modules exist, but the measured story here is ridge.

REFERENCE FIRST

Native Limen must stay native.

A fresh sklearn Ridge estimator for each call. No Terasweep cache transplanted into Limen. The small matched run exposes both a speed difference and backtest-semantic differences.

PROFILE → REMOVE → VECTORIZE

The scorer, not Cholesky, dominates.

93.1% of first-million score misses yield constant signals. Eliminating those scans changes the problem before any new SIMD is written.

INTEGRATE → SCALE → PRESERVE

From standalone kernels to a real pipeline.

Rust intrinsics and assembly share one runner. The 100k–1b study reveals cache saturation. The original and optimized implementations, raw outputs, and replay instructions are committed together.

MEASURED Recorded experiment PROJECTED Conditional reference-cost model TEACHING LAB Browser illustration, never benchmark evidence

All calculations and charts in the lesson are offline. No benchmark executes when you move a slider. Learning progress and notes stay in this browser when local storage is available. Evidence buttons open the retained reports or source snapshots; older reports keep their original limitations and deployment status.

chapters.title:
A reference you
can trust.
chapters.lead: Before optimizing anything, establish what is actually being compared. A native SFD is not a disguised cached implementation.
chapters.body:
Fresh estimator. Every time.

The merged Limen Ridge SFD delegates fitting and prediction to sklearn.linear_model.Ridge. Its train method constructs a new estimator and calls fit. In the native UEL path, preparation and the model execute again for every experiment row.

Changing only a fee does not cause the native reference to reuse the previous fit. That redundancy is precisely what the Terasweep sweep architecture can eliminate.

LIMEN · PINNED REFERENCE BEHAVIOR
self.model = _ridge(params)
self.model.fit(data['x_train'], data['y_train'])

# _ridge constructs sklearn.linear_model.Ridge.
# No cross-trial fit or prediction cache.

Limen merge commit 44eff3b2, PR #826. The wrapper is minimal; native preparation, metrics, Trainer and Sensor remain Limen responsibilities.

1,014native fit calls in the matched grid
6unique model configurations
169fee × slippage combinations per model

Same parameters do not mean the same work boundary.

Native CLI / UELraw input → prepare → fresh sklearn fit → predict → native metrics → full round artifacts
Terasweepprepared matrices → shared statistics → cached fits → cached/factored scores → winner summary

A native-relative application comparison is useful, but it is not a pure Python-versus-Rust, solver-versus-solver, or equal-output benchmark. The original Rust internal timer includes statistics, fit/predict precomputation, the sampled loop and winner details; it excludes input loading and price-statistics preparation. Whole-process timings avoid dividing those unlike sub-timers.

Economic equivalence was not established.

Terasweep uses entry-bar open-to-close returns and its existing multiplicative cost factors. Current native Limen uses its own entry and fees-on-notional convention. Rounded MAE and aggregate signal rates can match while return accounting differs. We preserved the original Rust contract instead of silently rewriting the reference.

Three workloads. Keep them separate.

EXPERIMENT MAPRECORDED INPUTS

Different hosts also appear at different stages: M1 Max for the early local work; an AMD EPYC guest for the first AVX-512 prototype; an Intel 8573C guest for the handwritten-kernel experiment; an Intel 8370C guest for integration; and an AMD EPYC 9V74 guest for scaling. Each report identifies its host. None of those host-to-host changes is an optimization gain.

CHECK YOUR MODEL

What does “six unique model configurations” tell you about native Limen’s 1,014-row grid?

Correct distinction: parameter identity is not call count. The uncached native loop fits every row. Cached Terasweep can fit each distinct training key once.

chapters.title:
Shrink the repeated
mathematics.
chapters.lead: Start with the ridge objective, not the estimator API. Identify the terms that do not change when the model parameters change.
chapters.body:
minw,b ‖y − Xw − b1‖² + α‖w‖²

Let n be training rows, d features, and m test rows. Without an intercept, the normal equations are (XᵀX + αI)w = Xᵀy. The dependence on the full training data is concentrated in two objects:

GRAM MATRIXG = XᵀXd × d values
RIGHT-HAND SIDEh = Xᵀyd values

For a new regularization strength, solve (G + αI)w = h. Neither G nor h changes with α. Terasweep computes them once, not once per logical sweep row. This was already present in the inherited implementation.

Derive the intercept path

Center the data: Xc = X − 1x̄ᵀ and yc = y − ȳ1. Form Gc = XcᵀXc and hc = Xcᵀyc. Solve (Gc + αI)w = hc, then recover b = ȳ − x̄ᵀw. The original code retains both raw and centered statistics and accumulates only the lower triangle before mirroring it for the solve.

The intercept is not penalized in this formulation. Changing the intercept setting chooses the relevant statistics; it does not require re-reading the training data for every trial.

A 55-feature problem remains a 55-feature problem.

The original training matrix is 4,136 × 55. Its repeated solve is a 55 × 55 system. One FP64 Gram matrix contains 24,200 bytes, calculated as 55 × 55 × 8. No feature is discarded.

Cholesky produces A = LLᵀ; forward and backward substitution solve the system. The code does not explicitly invert the matrix. It still performs a distinct Cholesky solve for each training key—there is no shared eigendecomposition across all α values in this implementation.

THE REUSE BOUNDARY

Fixed X and y.

A different feature set, scaler, split, window, target or dataset changes the statistics. Reuse is justified by dependencies, not resemblance.

The code’s solver_eps tests a Cholesky pivot. It is not sklearn’s iterative-solver tol. A failed solve is cached as a failed configuration, not converted to a successful model.

LAB / REGULARIZATION WITHOUT REBUILDING GTEACHING FIXTURE

Eight illustrative (x, y) pairs; one feature. This browser calculation is not market data or a performance measurement.

Predictions are another reusable intermediate.

Once a fit succeeds, the original code computes predictions and MAE in a single pass, storing them under (alpha.to_bits(), fit_intercept, solver_eps.to_bits()). A fee or threshold change cannot change those predictions.

O(nd²) + O(Ud³) + O(Umd)

Leading-order structural work for statistics, U distinct solves, and their test predictions. This is a complexity explanation, not a fitted timing model. It omits parsing, allocations, failure branches, scoring and reporting.

CHECK YOUR MODEL

You double the number of fee settings, keeping data and model parameters fixed. Which mathematical work must be repeated?

The model objective and its sufficient statistics do not depend on the fee. Fee evaluation changes the scoring stage, not the fitted coefficients.

chapters.title:
An experiment row
is not a job.
chapters.lead: One requested row can share almost all its expensive work with thousands of other rows. Factor at the intermediate-result boundary, not only at the final-output boundary.
chapters.body:
LAB / WHAT DOES THIS PARAMETER INVALIDATE?DEPENDENCY MODEL

Choose a change. The highlighted stages must be reconsidered; upstream unaffected stages remain reusable.

The original keys describe the actual dependencies.

IntermediateIdentity, with data fixedReused across
Training statisticsPrepared X and yAll model and score settings
Fit, predictions, MAEα, intercept, pivot cutoffRules, thresholds, fees, slippage
Base scoreTraining key, rule, thresholdFees and slippage
Cost-adjusted rowBase score plus fee and slippageNot globally memoized by the original runner

The full original scoring key deliberately excludes costs. That is not accidental omission: the inherited base-score statistics are designed so costs can be applied later. A complete-experiment cache would miss this sharing between different experiments.

384 × 2 × 32,304 configured training keys
627failed under the original pivot contract
1,677successful configured training keys

What a million rows really means.

The canonical million-row sample contained 728,102 valid rows and 271,898 failed-fit rows. There were 648,130 unique valid base-score keys. Training reuse was extensive, but only 79,972 valid rows reused a base score—about 11% of valid rows in that first million.

Do not let “cached sweep” suggest every row is cheap from the start. First encounters still cost work. Later chapters show what happens as the key space fills.

The sampler is deterministic, not unique.

SplitMix64 is seeded from the configured seed and a mixed row ID. An ID determines its parameters, which also lets the summary reconstruct a winner later. Sampling is with replacement. One billion requested rows is not one billion distinct configurations; the original configured Cartesian space contains 781,088,256 logical combinations, including failures.

Count failures honestly.

Once a training key fails, downstream requests reuse that failure. They remain part of the requested-row total and failure count. Throughput expressed as sampled rows per second therefore includes these cheaper failed requests. Calling it models trained per second would change the meaning of the benchmark.

CHECK YOUR MODEL

Which key is sufficient for a base score under the inherited contract?

The path depends on predictions, rule and threshold, with the price series fixed. Costs are applied to the retained path statistics afterward.

chapters.title:
Price the path.
Don’t replay the path.
chapters.lead: The original implementation does more than memoize. It derives compact statistics that support repeated fee/slippage evaluation without rescanning the bars.
chapters.body:
Separate the trading path from its costs.

Predictions, a rule, and a threshold determine the shifted position path. The original scorer uses the previous bar’s prediction for the current position, subject to tradability. Entry, continuation and exit flags determine the gross return and cost category.

aₜ = 1 + rₜgross   ·   Egross = ∏ₜ aₜ

Under Terasweep’s own cost convention, with fee f and slippage s expressed as fractions:

ENTRY MULTIPLIERu = (1 − f) / (1 + s)
EXIT MULTIPLIERv = (1 − f)(1 − s)
Enet = Egross · uentries · vexits

A new cost pair changes a few arithmetic operations, not the whole time-series traversal. These equations are not a claim about current Limen’s different accounting.

Sharpe needs moments, not only compounded return.

For each of four entry/exit categories, retain a count n꜀, a sum S꜀ = Σaₜ, and a squared sum Q꜀ = Σaₜ². Their cost multipliers are 1, u, v, uv. Since the net bar return is k꜀aₜ − 1:

Σrnet = Σ꜀ (k꜀S꜀ − n꜀)
Σ(rnet)² = Σ꜀ (k꜀²Q꜀ − 2k꜀S꜀ + n꜀)

Those two moments and the eligible-bar count give the mean and sample variance. The cost-adjustment stage operates over four categories. It does not require rebuilding the returns array for each fee setting.

LAB / ONE PATH, MANY COSTS12-BAR TEACHING FIXTURE

Illustrative prices and signals; original Terasweep formulas. Not a benchmark or a trading recommendation. The active position is shifted by one bar.

CategoryBarsΣaΣa²Cost factor

Not every diagnostic belongs in every trial.

These moments do not preserve an arbitrary drawdown path, rolling-return distribution, or trade-level quantile. Terasweep selects winners using the compact per-row metrics, then recomputes rich backtest details for the best return, best Sharpe and best MAE rows.

Three report slots need not mean three distinct winners. Selecting on rounded metrics also means ties must retain the original ordering. This is a summary-producing runner, not a replacement for full native per-trial artifact production.

CHECK YOUR MODEL

Can four category moments reconstruct arbitrary drawdown episodes?

The aggregate moments lose temporal ordering. The runner performs the richer path calculation for selected rows after the sweep rather than pretending the compact score contains every diagnostic.

chapters.title:
The bottleneck
was not the solver.
chapters.lead: Before writing instructions, measure where the existing program spends its time. The first major new optimization removed work rather than vectorizing it.
chapters.body:
A diagnostic, not a new denominator.

Sampling the original M1 executable pointed to score_cached. A diagnostic copy gave the inlined scorer a name and added phase timers. The resulting times are not an exact decomposition of the production binary, but they decisively identify the first target.

The source and historical executable remained unchanged. The diagnostic summary still matched the golden result.

M1 MAX · DIAGNOSTIC BUILD
Training statistics0.010 s
Fit and prediction0.098 s
Sampled loop4.179 s
Winner details0.00078 s

Phase timings are specific to this instrumented run. They are not pooled with later Intel/AMD process timings.

93.1% of score misses had one of two answers.

ALL OFF
ALL ON
394,015all-off logical keys
209,555all-on logical keys
44,560mixed logical keys

For a finite prediction vector, retain its minimum and maximum, plus those of its absolute values. For p > t, max(p) ≤ t proves all-off; min(p) > t proves all-on. Strict and inclusive inequalities matter at the exact boundary.

LAB / PROVE THE CONSTANT PATTERNILLUSTRATIVE PREDICTIONS

The first actual occurrence of each constant pattern is passed through the original scorer. Later constant keys reuse its exact payload. Non-finite prediction vectors fall back to the scalar path. For this million-row sample, full base-score scans fall from 648,130 to 44,562: 44,560 mixed paths and the two initial constant paths.

ISOLATED M1 PROTOTYPE
4.01 sOriginal median
→
0.77 sBounds-shortcut median
5.21×

Three alternating pairs. All 603,570 shortcuts were separately checked against the original scorer, field-for-field and float-bit-for-float-bit. The golden comparisons passed. This gain did not require new SIMD.

The new profile is a new problem.

After the shortcut, sampling showed meaningful hash lookup, insertion and rehash overhead. The first prototype still stored a full base-score payload under every logical key, even when hundreds of thousands of keys shared one of two values. Faster arithmetic was no longer the only opportunity.

CHECK YOUR MODEL

Why not start with handwritten Cholesky assembly?

The decision is workload-specific. The profile points to scoring first; once that is reduced, fitting can become a larger fraction of the remaining time. Optimize the current bottleneck, not a permanently favored kernel.

chapters.title:
Same logical result.
Smaller physical state.
chapters.lead: A cache is an algorithm and a memory layout. Preserving every logical key does not require storing a complete payload for every key.
chapters.body:
Three kinds of slot.

The inherited BaseScore is 128 bytes; its key is 24 bytes in the measured build. The compact path uses a logical key to select either the shared all-off result, the shared all-on result, or an individually stored mixed result.

The reported cache cardinality remains the number of logical keys. Compression changes physical representation, not what counts as an evaluated configuration.

LOGICAL ID → PHYSICAL PAYLOAD
0       → shared all-off BaseScore
1       → shared all-on BaseScore
2 + j   → mixed BaseScore[j]

row     → { train: u32, slot: u32 }

Actual allocation includes metadata, optional values, capacity slack, indexing and buffers. A payload-only calculation is not process RSS.

Use categorical identities when the configuration gives them to you.

The sampler already chooses positions in finite parameter arrays. Carry those ordinals forward rather than hashing float bit patterns on every normal generated row. Duplicate configured values still need their original deduplication semantics. Explicit CSV plans use lookup paths that retain the value-based contract.

A dense index is allowed only while its address space fits the 64 MiB cap; larger configured spaces use a sparse map with bounded initial reservation. “Use an array” is not a license to allocate the full theoretical grid without checking its size.

LAB / WHY A BILLION ROWS NEED NOT FILL MEMORYROW-REFERENCE STORAGE CALCULATION

Two u32 values per row reference: 8 bytes. The scheduler keeps at most 1,048,576 requested row references at a time. These values exclude all other storage; they are not measured RSS.

Cache state survives across blocks. Pending mixed jobs are grouped by model inside each block; rows are reduced in their original sequence afterward. Physical execution order may change, but rounded ties still favor the original earliest row.

939.1 MiBOriginal Rust peak RSS at 1b, AMD scaling run
77.8 MiBAssembly pipeline peak RSS at 1b, same study
224,178mixed states at full key-space coverage

The measured reduction reflects the complete implementation, not merely the row buffer. At full coverage the compact cache still retains state for distinct keys. “Bounded row scheduling” does not mean constant total memory for every possible configuration space.

A subtle cost remains.

The compact implementation samples each logical row during planning and again during original-order reduction. It applies costs and updates winners for every row. These operations become dominant after the score cache saturates; they are not erased by the SIMD kernel.

CHECK YOUR MODEL

Why is “only 44,560 mixed payloads” not the same as “only 44,560 logical score keys”?

Physical deduplication and logical accounting are different. The constant cases remain requested and scored; only duplicate payload storage is removed.

chapters.title:
Eight jobs.
One timeline.
chapters.lead: AVX-512 gives eight FP64 lanes. The engineering question is what a lane should represent—not merely whether wide registers exist.
chapters.body:
TEMPTING AXIS

Eight consecutive bars.

Comparisons vectorize naturally. But the equity product and category sums reduce across time. Reordering those floating-point reductions can change results. Vector width does not remove the temporal dependency.

CHOSEN AXIS

Eight independent score jobs.

Each lane carries its own threshold and rule, for the same fitted model. Broadcast one prediction and price row to all lanes. Advance through bars sequentially inside every lane.

This shares input loads while preserving each job’s chronological arithmetic. Category updates target separate lane-owned accumulators, avoiding several lanes scattering into the same four scalar sums. It creates useful parallel work without a horizontal reduction across time.

LAB / STEP THROUGH THE VECTOR12-BAR TEACHING FIXTURE

Each column is an independent score job. Signal uses the current prediction; position uses the previous signal and the current bar’s tradability. Active lanes retain separate state.

Why the first AVX-512 kernel tied AVX2.

Batching required both the same model and the same rule. Many groups did not fill eight lanes. With only 52.7% useful AVX-512 lanes, the first wide kernel’s median was 83.4 ms, essentially the same as the 83.6 ms AVX2 version.

Historical C prototype groupingAVX2 useful lanesAVX-512 useful lanesAVX-512 median
Same model, same rule73.9%52.7%83.4 ms
Same model, mixed rules94.5%88.3%60.3 ms

Allowing different rules within the same-model batch increased lane utilization. A per-lane sign transform handles less-than rules; an absolute-value mask handles absolute rules; an inclusive mask adds equality cases. The final Rust kernel carries the same idea.

The prototype language is not the final language.

The early x86 environment had C compilers but no Rust toolchain. A C reference enabled an exploratory SIMD experiment; it was separately checked against the original Rust scorer on the Mac. That experiment measured kernels, not the full Rust runner. The integrated pipeline later replaced that bridge with Rust std::arch::x86_64 intrinsics. There is no C scoring implementation in the final runtime.

Build for the verified instruction set.

The original Mac is ARM64; it cannot natively execute this x86 AVX-512 code. The integrated AVX-512 build targets x86-64 Linux with Rust 1.89 or newer. Runtime dispatch checks AVX-512F, and also BMI1 for the authored assembly. Unsupported levels fail rather than silently falling back. The Linux assembly ABI was not ported to x86 macOS or Windows.

CHECK YOUR MODEL

Why allow different rules within a same-model SIMD batch?

Mixed-rule packing increases useful-lane utilization without changing the underlying requested jobs or trading convention. The broader groups share the same fitted model.

chapters.title:
Make the incremental
claim real.
chapters.lead: “AVX-512” does not mean “handwritten assembly.” The final claim requires an authored kernel and an A/B that changes only that kernel.
chapters.body:
Do not compare against a convenient weak baseline.

The first handwritten variant looked faster than the early intrinsics implementation. Further intrinsics tuning recovered much of that gap. The standalone study compared multiple intrinsics formulations under GCC and Clang before selecting the strongest tested candidate.

“Strongest tested” is deliberately narrower than “the best intrinsics implementation possible.” The evidence does not prove assembly is inherently faster or that a compiler could never generate an equivalent schedule.

CODE WALK / THE AUTHORED KERNELACTUAL COMMITTED SOURCE


The actual integration boundary.
RUST LINKS BOTH KERNELS INTO ONE EXECUTABLE
core::arch::global_asm!(
    include_str!("score8_gpr.S"), options(raw)
);

let kernel: Kernel = if assembly {
    score8_asm_gpr
} else {
    score8_rust_intrinsics
};
Both functions receive the same packed thresholds, sign/absolute-value masks and price view. They write the same output layout. Grouping, packing, caching, cost adjustment and summary reduction stay in the same Rust pipeline. The extern "C" notation specifies a calling convention; it does not introduce a C implementation.


Three numbers that must not be confused.
STANDALONE · INTEL 8573C
1.070×
54.547 → 50.997 ms. Approx. 7% more scoring throughput, or 6.51% less time. The C-wrapper kernel experiment; not yet Rust end-to-end.
INTEGRATED · INTEL 8370C
1.0406×
770.530 → 740.476 ms. Ratio of medians for 16 full-process pairs. Assembly wins 12/16. The interval reaches effectively no whole-process gain.
1B SCALE · AMD 9V74
≈0.60%
98.8745 → 98.2869 s in one pair of full runs. Too little replication to establish a durable assembly-specific gain at this scale.


These are separate experiments, on different guests and scopes. They are not three factors to multiply. Their common lesson is that the end-to-end benefit depends on how much time still belongs to the optimized kernel.


What the assembly controls.
It explicitly assigns vector accumulators, keeps position-state masks in 32-bit general-purpose registers, transfers masks into AVX-512 mask registers, and schedules Boolean work alongside floating-point accumulation. It preserves separate multiplies and adds and chronological reduction within each lane. No FMA substitution, reduced precision or fast-math explains the gain.


CHECK YOUR MODEL
A kernel goes from 54.55 ms to 51.00 ms. What does “7% faster” mean here?
Throughput gain is old_time/new_time − 1. Time reduction is 1 − new_time/old_time. The whole-program effect depends on the fraction of runtime spent in that kernel.

chapters.title:
A faster wrong answer
is still wrong.
chapters.lead: Correctness is a hierarchy of claims. A golden summary, bitwise agreement, and economic equivalence are different tests.
chapters.body:
01

Same input identity

Hash the frozen matrices, configuration, source and executable. A filename alone is not a reproducibility contract.

02

Prediction and signal checks

Matching a rounded MAE or positive-signal count does not prove equal prediction arrays or equal signal positions. The integrated matched grid exported predictions: maximum observed difference 4.156 × 10⁻¹³, with all six complete sign vectors equal.

03

Complete intermediate results

A BaseScore contains eight integer fields and nine floating-point fields. Compare integer values and FP64 bit patterns, not only the final winners.

04

Full output and boundary behavior

Validate stable JSON, failure counts, rounded ties, strict/inclusive thresholds, signed zero, tail lanes, prefixes and tradability masks. Cross the 1,048,576-row block boundary.

05

Know the claim that still fails

Original-versus-optimized Rust equivalence does not establish current Limen backtest equivalence. Different economic conventions remain different even when model predictions agree.

3,364,062complete BaseScores checked per SIMD path at scale
17fields compared exactly per result
138,240Rust boundary comparisons on the scaling host

The large validation runs deliberately recompute scalar scores. They happened after the timed scaling runs and are excluded from the timing table. Exhausting this retained finite score-key universe is strong evidence for that workload, not a proof for every future input.

Measurement is also part of correctness.

Keep a ledger of boundaries.

Whole-process: launch, imports or input reading, computation, writes, exit. Internal timer: only the explicitly delimited stages. Kernel experiment: its stated grouping/packing/scoring scope. Never silently divide one by another.

Keep inconvenient observations.

Short-run stage times are not monotonic. Shared-VM outliers remain. An early timeout-wait pilot biased process timing and was excluded as a whole protocol for every variant, not cherry-picked per winner.

Claim clinic

Classify each sentence. “Unsupported” does not mean the code is bad; it means the sentence asks the evidence to establish something it did not test.

The benchmark is not a trading-quality result.

The optimization studies measure execution and agreement with a retained computational contract. They do not establish profitability, predictive generalization, data quality across markets, or live trading performance.

chapters.title:
Every level needs
its own denominator.
chapters.lead: Inspect the actual ablations. One study isolates the reuse levels; another measures the complete million-row pipeline. Neither needs a manufactured monotonic story.
chapters.body:
EXPLORER / INTEGRATED RUST EXPERIMENTINTEL XEON 8370C

The clean factorization comparison is within Rust.

On the 1,014-row grid, turning statistics, prediction and score reuse on reduces the internal timer from 511.384 ms to 4.440 ms: 115.18×. The prepared input and Rust scoring/output contract stay the same.

The full native CLI median of 31.280 s divided by the original cached Rust process median of 28.887 ms gives about 1,083×. That ratio includes differences in preparation, orchestration, metrics and artifacts. It is not a 1,083× solver gain.

WHY THE LAST STAGES PLATEAU

Six models. Six paths.

All 1,014 rows collapse to six fits and six scoring paths. Each model supplies only one scoring job, leaving most SIMD lanes unused. Only six path evaluations remain after caching. Startup and scheduling dominate the final differences.

The input also has 1,430 positive predictions out of 1,431 for each native model. That observed property limits how well this grid represents a varied scoring workload.

The million-row study tests the later optimizations.

On the original 55-feature workload, the integrated pipeline’s five-stage process median falls from 6.942 s to 0.758 s—9.16× versus original Rust on that host. The dedicated assembly A/B uses separate paired runs and reports its own median, not a substituted value from the five-stage table.

That distinction explains why you will see 0.758 s in the multi-stage study and 0.740 s in the paired assembly study. They are measurements from different protocols, not interchangeable cells.

CHECK YOUR MODEL

Can you multiply the 1,083× native-grid ratio by the 9.16× million-row Rust ratio?

A cumulative end-to-end claim needs a common workload, machine and timing boundary. These two ratios are both useful, but multiplying them fabricates a measurement that was never made.

chapters.title:
Watch the multiplier
grow—and flatten.
chapters.lead: Twenty-five actual Rust processes, 100k through 1b sampled rows. Only the large native-reference runtimes are inferred.
chapters.body:
EXPLORER / 5,555,500,000 ACTUAL RUST ROW EVALUATIONSAMD EPYC 9V74

Every plotted Rust point is a fresh-process measurement with empty computational caches. One run per stage/size; no outliers removed. Lines connect observations for readability, not to invent measurements between them. OS file caches were not flushed.

The growth is real. The denominator is modeled.

The same-matrix native Ridge reference was calibrated with 256 and 2,048 evaluations, twice each, using a fresh sklearn fit and native metrics every time. Its fitted reference-cost model is:

TLimen prepared(N) = 0.120492 + 0.006253191N seconds

That intercept belongs to the prepared-loop calibration, not Python/import startup. Those overheads are excluded from the prepared reference’s loop timing, while every plotted Rust denominator includes its whole process. The full native CLI reference includes its entire process but uses a separate 13-feature workflow, not the original 55-feature matrices.

At 1b, the measured assembly process is 98.286879 s. The projected same-matrix native Ridge cost is about 72.37 days, giving about 63,622×. This is explicitly a projected reference-cost multiplier; native signal rules and solver-failure contracts are not replaced with the Rust scorer.

The large native jobs were not run.

Linearity is an assumption requested for this study. Short-run calibration variability and long-run memory, artifact I/O and scheduler effects are not resolved by a straight line. The two prepared-native repetitions imply slopes of about 5.897 and 6.609 ms/row. The chart uses the recorded central model, not a confidence guarantee.

Cache saturation explains the shape.

The 1,677 successful training keys each have 2,006 rule/threshold possibilities: 4 × 401 + 2 × 201. The valid base-score-key ceiling is therefore 3,364,062. It is already reached at 100m rows in this sample. At 1b, about 99.54% of valid rows reuse a base score.

TRust(N) ≈ fixed training + c · unique scores(N) + dN

This is an explanatory structural model, not a substitute for the actual Rust timings. Once unique scores stop increasing, the remaining per-row term still grows. The multiplier approaches a ceiling; it does not become infinite.

The last bottleneck has moved again.

Planning, sampling and cache lookup at 1b53.805 s
Costs and summary reduction44.016 s
Mixed scoring, grouping and packing0.336 s

The scoring kernel’s phase is now only 0.342% of whole-process time. The native-relative multiplier can grow while the intrinsics and handwritten curves converge. Assembly has little opportunity to help after its work is mostly reused.

LAB / WHERE CAN THE NEXT SPEEDUP COME FROM?AMDAHL CALCULATION
Swhole = 1 / [(1 − p) + p / s]

This is a calculation using a chosen target share and speedup, not a new measurement. It assumes all other work remains unchanged. At p = 100%, the infinite-kernel limit is unbounded in the mathematical model.

CHECK YOUR MODEL

Why can original Rust catch up to the optimized scorer as N becomes huge?

Both implementations eventually reuse nearly every valid base score. Faster first-time scoring is then a smaller fraction of total runtime, so its incremental whole-program contribution shrinks.

chapters.lead: The investigation is not complete when a chart exists. The code, data, environment, validation, limits and replay path must survive outside the working session.
chapters.body:
The Git handoff is the durable boundary.

The original source is preserved as baseline-2026-05. The integrated runtime is commit 70525ba. The verified experiment snapshot is benchmark-handoff-2026-09-24 at 2e549d4, including reports, raw records, archives and integrity checks. This course is an additive teaching layer; it does not revise those measurements.

Open the evidence, then replay deliberately.

The repository keeps readable reports in benchmarks/reports/, original experiment bundles in benchmarks/archives/, earlier prototypes and the C oracle in benchmarks/mac-history/, and handoff checks in benchmarks/handoff/. Compiler installers, Python environments and duplicate clean worktrees are rebuildable dependencies, not the unique research record.

VERIFY THE PRESERVED EVIDENCE
git clone https://github.com/mikkokotila/Terasweep.git
cd Terasweep
python3 scripts/verify_evidence.py

# Use a separate clean checkout for the original snapshot:
git worktree add ../Terasweep-baseline baseline-2026-05

The repository is private; access uses your existing GitHub authorization. Nothing in this lesson bypasses that requirement.

RUN THE INTEGRATED LEVELS · DISTINCT OUTPUT DIRECTORIES
make build
make run LEVEL=compact RUNS=1000000 OUT=runs/lesson-compact

# On supported x86-64 Linux with Rust 1.89+:
make run LEVEL=intrinsics RUNS=1000000 OUT=runs/lesson-intrinsics
make run LEVEL=assembly RUNS=1000000 OUT=runs/lesson-assembly
make test
TERASWEEP_CHECK_BASE=1 make verify LEVEL=assembly

Do not include TERASWEEP_CHECK_BASE=1 in performance measurements: it recomputes the oracle. make verify creates a fresh output directory. make run writes to the selected output path, so choose a new path when retaining observations. The bare executable defaults to score; the Makefile defaults to compact. Unsupported SIMD selections fail rather than posing as assembly runs.

The end-to-end method

Freeze the contract→Factor dependencies→Profile→Remove redundant work→Compact the state→Choose SIMD lanes→Schedule instructions→Validate and scale→Commit the evidence

That order matters. Handwritten assembly is a final, specific intervention—not the explanation for the huge native-relative multiplier. The large ratio largely reflects avoiding repeated work. The instruction-level increment is real only to the extent that an appropriately controlled A/B measures it.

CAPSTONE / WRITE THE CLAIM YOU WOULD SIGNSYNTHESIS

Write a short results paragraph that includes the actual billion-row time, its sampled-row meaning, the native projection boundary, the assembly-specific limit, and one reproducibility detail.

Compare with a defensible synthesis

On a single pinned CPU in the recorded AMD EPYC 9V74 VM, the integrated Rust/handwritten-assembly pipeline processed one billion sampled rows in 98.286879 seconds. This includes cached failed-fit rows and is not one billion independent model fits. A short-run linear native Ridge cost model on the same matrices implies approximately 63,622× relative throughput; that native large run was not executed, and the scoring contracts differ. The one-pair intrinsics/assembly difference at this scale is not an established assembly-specific gain. Earlier paired integration measurements support a small, noisy whole-pipeline increment. Source, frozen inputs, validation records and replay scripts are preserved in the benchmark handoff snapshot.

What remains open—not what was silently solved.

The record does not establish complete current-Limen/Terasweep economic equivalence, a universal assembly advantage, linear native billion-row feasibility, live trading quality, or unlimited scaling. At saturation, sampling, lookups, costs and reduction are the obvious measured targets to investigate next; accelerating them is future work, not part of these results.

First change how much work exists.
Then change how fast you execute what remains.
Open the verified Git snapshot ↗

# Native Limen versus Terasweep — measured results

Run date: 22 September 2026. All measurements below came from execution on the connected Mac, not estimates or extrapolations.

## Scope

Two unchanged implementations were executed:

- Native Limen 5.11.0 at merged commit `44eff3b244c80ce8473845bd60b074b3682fe441`, through its actual `python -m limen run` CLI, YAML compiler, manifest preparation, UEL, Ridge SFD, inline metrics, and artifact writing.
- The existing `~/dev/Terasweep/target/terasweep` executable. No rebuild or source change was made.

The matched workload was the newly shipped Ridge SFD's six cases: alpha 0.1, 1.0, and 10.0, each with and without an intercept. This is NOT a one-million-round native-Limen-versus-Terasweep benchmark. The original Terasweep 1M workload was rerun separately and was not used to calculate a cross-engine speedup.

The original sweep contains solver-pivot tolerances and signal-rule/threshold variations that the native Ridge SFD does not implement. No substitute SFD, custom solver, custom backtest, or cache was introduced to simulate that original sweep inside Limen.

## Inputs and matching

The shipped native YAML template was changed only to use a frozen local source, deterministic native grid enumeration, and output paths. Model parameters, feature preparation, target, scaling, and native evaluation remained those of the shipped template.

- Raw data: 8,760 BTCUSDT hourly observations, 1 January–31 December 2025.
- Source: the already-cached `btcusdt_1h_kline_20200101_to_20260921.parquet` snapshot, read through native `HistoricalData.get_any_file`; the 2025 observations were retained as `raw.parquet`.
- Native prepared training shape: 6,521 × 22.
- Native prepared validation shape: 1,439 × 22.
- Native prepared test shape: 719 × 22; 719 matching open/close price pairs.
- Native training resolves `solver='auto'` to Cholesky in all six cases.
- Native signal: prediction > 0; native default costs: 5 bps fee and 5 bps slippage per fill.
- The exact native-prepared training/test arrays and prices were serialized into Terasweep's existing binary format. Exported matrices were read back and checked for exact equality.
- Terasweep configuration: the same three alphas and two intercept settings; `gt`, threshold 0, fee 5, slippage 5, `solver_eps=1e-12`. Native `tol` was not equated to Terasweep's pivot cutoff.
- Terasweep seed 20260698 makes the first six sampled rows cover all six combinations once. Its measured summary confirms six training configurations, six score-cache entries, six valid rows, and no failures.

Native validation data is retained by its pipeline but is not used to fit Ridge. Terasweep consumes only the training/test matrices and prices, as its normal interface specifies.

## Timings

Five separate-process repeats, with alternating engine order. No runs were discarded.

| Repeat | Native CLI wall time, s | Terasweep wall time, s | Sum of native logged round times, s | Terasweep internal timer, s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 2.84 | 0.02 | 0.32 | 0.003459208 |
| 2 | 2.34 | 0.01 | 0.29 | 0.003115333 |
| 3 | 2.46 | 0.01 | 0.35 | 0.003071750 |
| 4 | 2.33 | 0.01 | 0.37 | 0.003106458 |
| 5 | 2.40 | 0.01 | 0.24 | 0.003545583 |
| Median | 2.40 | 0.01 | 0.32 | 0.003115333 |

Median peak resident memory: native Limen 255.375 MiB; Terasweep 4.40625 MiB.

Wall timing used `/usr/bin/time -lp`, whose saved output resolves seconds to two decimals. The 0.01-second Terasweep readings do not justify a precise wall-time speedup factor.

These are different pipeline boundaries. Native CLI wall time includes Python startup/imports, YAML validation, raw loading, repeated manifest preparation, fitting, native metrics, and complete experiment artifacts. Terasweep reads already-prepared arrays, reuses training sufficient statistics, and writes its summary. Its internal timer includes preparation of ridge statistics and fits/predictions, scoring, and winner details, but excludes input loading. The native logged round timers include preparation and native metric computation and are also rounded. Neither timer isolates the ridge solver. No pure ridge-fit speedup is claimed.

This six-case run has no repeated score-cache hits: six rows produce six unique score keys. It therefore does not establish large-sweep scaling or steady-state cache throughput.

The machine was busy: the one-minute load average at the beginning of the measured sequence was 27.65. Other users' processes were not stopped. These are observed timings under contention, not an isolated-machine performance ceiling.

## Output agreement

All six cases have reported MAE 0.290 in both implementations, and all six agree on reported positive-signal rate.

| Alpha | Intercept | Positive predictions, both | Signal rate, both, % | Native compounded return rounded to 0.1%, % | Terasweep reported return, % |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | Yes | 310 | 43.115 | -26.5 | -26.5 |
| 1.0 | Yes | 313 | 43.533 | -24.5 | -24.4 |
| 10.0 | Yes | 335 | 46.592 | -22.3 | -22.3 |
| 0.1 | No | 314 | 43.672 | -23.4 | -23.4 |
| 1.0 | No | 318 | 44.228 | -24.4 | -24.4 |
| 10.0 | No | 335 | 46.592 | -22.3 | -22.3 |

Each Terasweep case was additionally executed as a singleton configuration for validation, outside the five timed comparisons. Terasweep signal counts in this table are recovered from its reported signal rate and the known 719-row denominator. They are not its differently defined `edge_per_signal_n` statistic.

Native compounded return is calculated from the per-bar net returns produced by Limen's existing `long_flat_strategy`, using the retained native predictions and the same prices and costs. It is a derived diagnostic, not a total-return field in native `results.csv`. Raw native values are retained in `comparison.json`.

The stock backtest implementations are not equivalent: Terasweep uses the entry bar's open-to-close return and its cached cost-factor formula; current Limen uses prior-close-to-close returns and its current fees-on-notional accounting. Their metric inventories and aggregation populations also differ. Five matching rounded total returns do not establish exact economic parity; one already differs at the shared display precision.

MAE/signal-rate agreement is aggregate, rounded-output agreement only. The unchanged Terasweep executable does not export the complete coefficient or prediction arrays, so full coefficient, prediction, or bar-by-bar signal parity was not established.

## Repeatability and native reconstruction

- All five native result tables are identical after excluding `execution_time`.
- All five native `round_data.jsonl` files, including predictions, are byte-identical.
- All five Terasweep summaries are identical after excluding the two timing fields.
- All six native models reconstruct through native `Trainer`, loading the frozen input from the retained YAML reference without a data-source monkeypatch.
- All six reconstructed Sensors return finite predictions. The stock sklearn feature-name warning is emitted during Sensor inference; it was not suppressed or patched.
- A further run using the saved replay command in a fresh output directory also reproduced native stable metrics, native prediction artifacts, and Terasweep stable output exactly. This replay is not included in the five-run timing table.

## Separate original Terasweep 1M regression run

Original, unchanged inputs and `configs/sweep.json`:

| Measurement | Result |
|---|---:|
| Sampled rows | 1,000,000 |
| Internal timer | 4.483524333 s |
| Process wall time | 4.50 s |
| Internal sampled-row throughput | 223,038.825203 rows/s |
| Valid rows | 728,102 |
| Failed rows | 271,898 |
| Unique training configurations | 2,304 |
| Failed training configurations | 627 |
| Golden comparison | Passed |

The failures match the saved canonical result. Sampled-row throughput includes failed rows and is not a count of independently fitted models per second. Native Limen was not run for this 1M workload, so there is no measured 1M cross-engine ratio.

## Environment

Apple M1 Max, arm64, 64 GiB RAM, macOS 26.6.2. Python 3.12.12; Limen 5.11.0; NumPy 2.5.1; SciPy 1.18.0; scikit-learn 1.9.0; Polars 1.42.1; pandas 2.3.3; PyArrow 22.0.0. These are the installed versions observed on the connected machine.

Both timed paths received `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1`, `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1`, `MKL_NUM_THREADS=1`, `VECLIB_MAXIMUM_THREADS=1`, and `NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS=1`. Polars' thread setting was not overridden.

## Retained evidence and replay

Everything needed for the executed comparison is retained on the connected Mac under:

`/Users/mikkokotila/dev/_reports/ridge-side-by-side-20260922/`

Key files: `provenance.json`, `timings.json`, `comparison.json`, `repeatability.json`, `input-sha256.txt`, `native-repeatable.yaml`, `terasweep.json`, `raw.parquet`, `train.bin`, `test.bin`, `price.bin`, and `replay.sh`. Original measurements and experiment artifacts are under `native/`, `terasweep/`, `logs/`, `validation/`, and `original-1m/`.

```sh
~/dev/_reports/ridge-side-by-side-20260922/replay.sh \
  "$HOME/dev/_reports/ridge-replay-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
```

The script checks input/executable hashes before running. It defaults to the exact Python environment used here; `LIMEN_PYTHON` can select another interpreter, whose package versions must be matched to the recorded environment for a comparable replay. It refuses an already-existing output directory rather than deleting previous results.

# Terasweep SIMD exploration — 22 September 2026

## Scope and evidence

This is an exploration of the existing original 1,000,000-row ridge workload, not a new Limen comparison. Work was performed on the connected Apple M1 Max. No AVX-512 instructions were executed. Limen and the production Terasweep sources/executable were not changed. All modified Rust sources and binaries are isolated under:

`/Users/mikkokotila/dev/_reports/terasweep-simd-20260922-u3uJGl/`

Machine-readable measurements accompany this report in `terasweep_simd_exploration.json`.

## Profiling

The original executable was sampled during one run. It completed in 4.17 seconds and passed the existing golden comparison. In the captured window, 3,115 of 3,300 top-of-stack samples were in `score_cached`, which includes inlined base-score work. Sampling started after process launch and missed early work; this is not a complete wall-time breakdown.

A diagnostic source copy added phase timers, named non-inlined scoring functions, and counters. Its output also passed the golden comparison. Phase times were:

| Phase | Seconds |
|---|---:|
| Training-statistics preparation | 0.010118333 |
| Fit/predict precomputation | 0.098406250 |
| Sampled sweep loop | 4.178596541 |
| Detailed winner reporting | 0.000777541 |

These times belong to an instrumented build, not an optimization ablation or an exact allocation of production wall time.

Original scoring disassembly shows scalar floating-point comparisons, indirect signal-rule dispatch within the scans, a serial equity product, and category-indexed moment updates. This identifies concrete control-flow and vectorization opportunities; it does not establish how the same source will compile on x86.

## Exact all-on/all-off shortcut

The 648,130 base-score cache misses divided into:

| Signal pattern | Count |
|---|---:|
| All off | 394,015 |
| All on | 209,555 |
| Mixed | 44,560 |

Thus 603,570 misses, or 93.1248%, correspond to one of two constant signal patterns.

An isolated prototype computes min/max prediction and absolute-prediction bounds once per encountered fitted configuration. For finite predictions, exact comparisons against those bounds detect all-off and all-on cases for all six signal rules. Non-finite prediction vectors use the original scorer.

The first actual occurrence of each constant pattern is evaluated with the original scorer. The resulting BaseScore is reused for later constant-pattern misses within the same fixed-data sweep. Mixed patterns still use the original scorer. All original score keys and cache-entry counts remain; candidate generation, fit failures, costs, winner selection, and reporting are unchanged.

No market data, targets, or predictions were fabricated. The shortcut is reuse of an already-computed result, not pruning or approximate scoring.

A validation run recomputed the original BaseScore for every shortcut and compared integer fields exactly and all floating-point fields by bit pattern. All 603,570 checks passed. The complete golden comparison passed as well. This proves parity for these encountered cases, not universal correctness for every possible future input.

## Unprofiled paired measurements

Same compiler/build options, same machine, same original data/config, separate processes. Execution order was original/prototype, prototype/original, original/prototype. Background activity was not stopped and CPU affinity was not controlled.

| Pair | Original wall seconds | Bounds prototype wall seconds |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 3.81 | 0.77 |
| 2 | 4.07 | 0.74 |
| 3 | 4.01 | 0.82 |
| Median | 4.01 | 0.77 |

The ratio of medians is 5.2078×. Every output passed golden validation. The first exploratory prototype run took 0.67 seconds; the paired median above is the appropriate headline, not that best observation.

Median instructions retired fell from 64,980,727,442 to 7,478,546,203. Median peak RSS remained approximately 345 MB because the prototype intentionally retained the original cache structure.

This is not an AVX-512 speedup. It is evidence for work elimination before SIMD.

## Residual bottleneck

A short sample of the prototype captured 601 stacks. Of these, 274 were in `compute_base_score`; 174 were in the listed hashing, insertion, and rehashing functions. Startup and training may be missed. These roughly 46% and 29% shares describe the captured window only.

A 10× improvement over the new paired original baseline would require 0.401 seconds. From the prototype's 0.77-second median, another 1.9202× total-program improvement is required. Because substantial work now lies outside base scoring, vectorizing only that kernel is not a reliable route to the whole target.

## Recommended AVX-512 design to test

First specialize signal-rule dispatch outside the bar loop and avoid repeated comparison of the same prediction. Then test SIMD lanes representing independent score jobs, preferably different requested thresholds of one model and rule. Eight FP64 lanes can process eight thresholds while broadcasting one prediction and one price row.

Keep time sequential within each lane. Each lane maintains its own equity product and four category-count/moment accumulators. Masked updates preserve inactive accumulators. This avoids reassociating the time-series reductions, unlike vectorizing eight successive bars and horizontally reducing them.

This design is a proposal, not implemented or benchmarked AVX-512 code. It needs checks for lane occupancy, register spills, batch-scheduling overhead, tails, non-finite values, and exact threshold boundaries. Preserve logical run IDs and rounded tie-breaking despite physical batching. Do not eagerly compute the entire theoretical score grid just to fill lanes.

A complementary cache change is important: constant scores need not occupy separate 128-byte payloads for every logical key. Keep logical-key accounting but store compact references/tags to the two shared constant scores and an arena of mixed scores. Only 44,560 observed mixed scores require distinct payloads in this workload. Compact categorical keys and elimination of avoidable training-key hashing should also be measured. Do not allocate a full dense score grid without a memory-cost calculation.

Cholesky and prediction SIMD come after re-profiling this reduced engine. Their roughly 0.1-second diagnostic precomputation cost becomes more significant against a 0.401-second total target, but optimizing them first would have targeted a small part of the original sweep.

## Hardware, compiler, and acceptance

Only the ARM Mac was connected through Remote Desktop Commander. Historical May hosted-runner probes do not establish a currently available AVX-512 machine. A real x86 host with runtime-verified features is required for native measurement; emulation cannot establish throughput.

The local compiler is rustc 1.63.0. Stable AVX-512 intrinsics and target features needed for a modern Rust implementation require a newer pinned toolchain; many were stabilized in 1.89.0. Do not silently update the user's default toolchain.

Compare scalar/specialized, AVX2, and AVX-512 implementations on the same x86 CPU using the same pinned toolchain and workload. Separate compiler, algorithm, ISA, and threading gains. Start with intrinsics and inspect generated assembly before adding handwritten assembly. Preserve the original arithmetic ordering first; no global fast-math, automatic FMA substitution, or FP32 conversion as an unlabelled optimization.

Validate intermediate score fields, signals, failure classifications, per-row metrics, and tie-breaking, not only final winners. Use same-platform scalar output as the SIMD oracle and investigate any cross-platform golden drift separately. Optimizing Terasweep does not repair the previously documented economic-semantics differences from native Limen.

## Retained evidence on the Mac

- `sample.txt`, `time.txt`, `summary.json`: original sampled run.
- `profile-src/`, `profile-sweep`, `profile-time.txt`, `profile-sample.txt`: phase/counter diagnostics.
- `score-original.asm`: original scorer disassembly.
- `bounds-src/`, `bounds-sweep`: isolated shortcut prototype.
- `bounds-check.txt`, `bounds-checked-summary.json`: all shortcut comparisons and golden-compatible result.
- `original-pair-*.time`, `bounds-pair-*.time`, corresponding JSON summaries: paired runs.
- `bounds-sample.txt`: residual sample.
- `exploration.json`: collected measurements.

## Primary technical references

- Intel, Intel AVX-512 Instructions: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/intel-avx-512-instructions.html
- Intel, Tuning SIMD vectorization: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/tuning-simd-vectorization-when-targeting-intel-xeon-processor-scalable-family.html
- LLVM, Auto-Vectorization: https://llvm.org/docs/Vectorizers.html
- Rust, masked FP64 addition: https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/arch/x86_64/fn._mm512_mask_add_pd.html
- Rust, runtime x86 feature detection: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/macro.is_x86_feature_detected.html
- Rust 1.89 release announcement: https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/07/Rust-1.89.0/

# AVX-512 scoring-kernel experiment — 22 September 2026

## Result and scope

The best tested AVX-512 implementation took **60.285 ms** to evaluate the original workload's **44,560 distinct mixed-signal base-score jobs**. Across 12 interleaved repetitions, this was **3.974× faster than the C reference scorer**, **3.396× faster than a specialized scalar C scorer**, and **1.299× faster than the best tested AVX2 implementation**.

These are **C kernel measurements, not end-to-end Rust Terasweep measurements**. No new native-Limen comparison or whole-sweep speedup is claimed.

The uploaded archive's SHA-256 matched the archive prepared on the Mac:

`6c1e549ff86b80446e2231e3f219760ae0fb746b38a91e1316bb4d0d3e1e4bc4`

## Why this is a C experiment

The x86 execution environment exposes AVX2 and AVX-512F and successfully executes the kernels. GCC 14.2.0 is installed. Rust is not installed, and attempts to download its toolchain into this environment failed. The unchanged Rust runner was therefore **not built or benchmarked here**.

Rather than substitute a new full-sweep runner and call it Terasweep, the experiment isolates the identified scoring bottleneck. Its C reference is a direct translation of the supplied `results.rs::compute_base_score`; preparation translates the supplied ridge normal-equation/Cholesky loops and sampling sequence to obtain workloads from the retained input matrices. This preparation is not a new production model and is excluded from kernel timings.

## Hardware and compilation

- Reported processor: AMD EPYC 9V74 80-Core Processor, x86-64, KVM guest.
- Guest exposes five logical CPUs and a four-CPU-equivalent quota, with a 4 GiB memory limit.
- Benchmark process pinned itself to logical CPU 0 and ran single-threaded.
- Compiler: GCC 14.2.0.
- Common options: `-O3 -g -march=x86-64-v3 -ffp-contract=off -fno-fast-math -Wall -Wextra`.
- Explicit SIMD functions have `target("avx2")` or `target("avx512f")` attributes.
- FP64 retained throughout; no fast-math, fused multiply-add substitution, or horizontal reassociation of the per-job temporal reductions.
- This is a shared virtual environment, not an isolated hardware-limit benchmark.

The compiled disassembly includes executed AVX-512 masked FP64 additions and vector multiplications, for example:

```asm
vaddpd zmm4{k2}, zmm6, QWORD BCST [r13+r10]
vaddpd zmm19{k1}, zmm19, zmm1
vmulpd zmm3, zmm3, zmm1
```

The experiment uses intrinsics. It does not use handwritten assembly.

## Workload identity

The supplied train/test/price files were used without alteration. They describe 4,136 training rows, 55 features, and 1,136 test/price rows. The experiment reconstructs the original configuration's seed 20260514, 384 log-spaced alphas, two intercept choices, three solver cutoffs, six signal rules, and signed/absolute threshold grids.

Observed counts match the previously recorded workload:

| Quantity | Count |
|---|---:|
| Training configurations | 2,304 |
| Failed training configurations | 627 |
| Failed sampled rows | 271,898 |
| Unique successful base-score keys | 648,130 |
| All-off keys | 394,015 |
| All-on keys | 209,555 |
| Mixed-signal keys | 44,560 |

Only the mixed-signal jobs are timed in this kernel experiment. Constant-pattern shortcut performance, hashing, cache representation, fee/slippage application, and full-sweep orchestration are not measured here. Matching these counts alone is not proof of all cross-platform prediction bits; numerical validation is described separately below.

## Timings

Each value below is for all 44,560 mixed-signal jobs. There were 12 repetitions, rotating the order of six implementations. Each implementation occupies every timing-order position twice. Validation executes each implementation before the timed sequence.

| Implementation | Median | Observed minimum–maximum | Speedup vs C reference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| C reference scorer | 239.565 ms | 219.412–255.650 ms | 1.000× |
| Specialized scalar C | 204.712 ms | 190.290–222.676 ms | 1.170× |
| AVX2, one model/rule per batch | 83.592 ms | 78.050–91.492 ms | 2.866× |
| AVX-512, one model/rule per batch | 83.368 ms | 78.254–89.490 ms | 2.874× |
| AVX2, one model with mixed rules per batch | 78.282 ms | 73.825–94.894 ms | 3.060× |
| AVX-512, one model with mixed rules per batch | 60.285 ms | 56.838–70.688 ms | 3.974× |

The source reference is compiled with the same optimization options as the other implementations. There is no forced no-vectorization flag to artificially slow it down. “Specialized scalar” describes its programming structure, not a promise that GCC emits no SIMD anywhere.

### Timing boundary

Included: grouping the already-sorted job sequence into batches, packing thresholds and lane-rule masks, evaluating base scores, and writing the complete outputs.

Excluded: loading files; forming training statistics; fitting and predicting; generating the one-million-row sample; classifying constant patterns; deduplicating and sorting jobs; correctness validation; fingerprinting outputs; cost application; winner selection; and experiment-artifact serialization.

Consequently these numbers cannot be substituted into the prior full-process Limen/Terasweep table.

## What changed between the two batching designs

### First design: eight thresholds for one model and one rule

Each lane holds a different threshold. All lanes share the current prediction and price values. The time axis remains sequential within each lane. Many model/rule groups are small, however.

Useful-lane utilization was **73.917% for AVX2** and **52.696% for AVX-512**. The wider implementation was effectively tied with AVX2.

### Improved design: eight requested score jobs for one model, allowing different rules

The batch can now cross rule boundaries while retaining the same fitted model and shared prediction loads. Lane masks encode whether a lane needs a strict/inclusive comparison, a sign reversal for less-than rules, or an absolute value.

Useful-lane utilization rose to **94.511% for AVX2** and **88.273% for AVX-512**. The best AVX-512 version is approximately 30% faster than the corresponding AVX2 version.

Every lane still accumulates its equity product and category moments in original chronological order. Entry/exit counts are reconstructed from category counts; their equality is included in validation. Tail lanes duplicate a valid threshold/rule internally, and only requested outputs are stored.

This result supports testing cross-rule, same-model batching in the Rust implementation. It does not establish that grouping/scheduling and cache costs will be negligible in an integrated runner.

## Correctness evidence

### Independent C-reference/Rust comparison on the Mac

A diagnostic copy of the **original Rust source** exported original predictions, precomputed prices, and the complete `compute_base_score` result for all **648,130 unique base-score keys** in the one-million-row sample. The same C reference-scoring function was compiled on the Mac with Clang using strict FP options and run against this fixture.

Observed result:

```text
Original Rust scorer exported 648130 unique base scores
C reference equals original Rust bit-for-bit: 648130 complete BaseScores, all 17 fields each
```

All eight integer fields and all nine floating-point bit patterns were compared, rather than just rounded final scores.

The retained validation is at:

`~/dev/_reports/terasweep-c-oracle-fU6UxO/`

The diagnostic copy and its 113 MB fixture are separate from the original project. This check establishes reference parity on the Mac. It is not a native-x86 Rust execution or an integrated-runner golden check.

### SIMD validation in the x86 environment

Each of the five optimized variants matched the C reference on every field of all **44,560 mixed-signal jobs**.

The same-rule AVX2 and AVX-512 kernels additionally passed **19,440 boundary jobs each**, using thresholds at selected real predictions, one representable value on either side, signed zero, and observed extrema.

The mixed-rule versions additionally passed **3,240 mixed-rule boundary jobs each**, using actual predictions and adjacent representable thresholds. The raw log's `boundary_validation.jobs_per_simd_mode` field refers to the 19,440 same-rule tests; the extra mixed-rule assertion loop is present in the source but does not print a separate counter.

All measured outputs had fingerprint `b4bba056c98c06c0`. Fingerprinting prevents unused results and checks repeat consistency; the full pre-timing bitwise comparison, not this fingerprint, is the substantive correctness test.

## Interpretation

The useful measured result is a **3.974× scoring-kernel speedup over the validated C reference**, with **1.299× specifically over the best AVX2 implementation tested**. Improved batching was necessary to make 512-bit width pay off.

There is no supported 10× whole-program claim. The earlier bounds shortcut was measured on an M1 Max, while these kernel measurements are on an x86 guest and cover a different timing boundary. Multiplying the two factors would not be a valid measured end-to-end result.

The required next measurement is the original Rust runner, the bounds/compact-cache scalar path, and integrated AVX2/AVX-512 paths built with one pinned x86 compiler and run on the same x86 machine, including all grouping, cache, cost, and reporting overhead.

## Offline Rust toolchain prepared on the Mac

The official Rust 1.89.0 x86-64 Linux compiler and standard-library archives were downloaded and checked against their published SHA-256 files. They have **not** been installed on the Mac and no default toolchain was changed.

Bundle:

`~/Downloads/terasweep-linux-toolchain-DUwjgC/rust-linux-offline.tar`

Reported size: 106 MB.

SHA-256:

`de9f039ba6db992f4e007c7cccc60833cc399d6847eb55eb65d6a07f60db78b8`

Uploading that bundle into the conversation enables the missing native-Rust build step without paying for another machine.

## Reproduction and evidence

The accompanying experiment archive includes the exact C source, original supplied inputs and source snapshots, input checksums, replay script, raw timing logs, compiler output, disassembly, environment record, and the recorded Mac oracle-validation result. The Mac's large oracle fixture and the compiler archives are not duplicated in the download.

Run `./replay.sh /absolute/path/to/a/new/output-directory` on compatible x86 Linux with GCC, Python, and AVX-512F. The script verifies the original input/configuration hashes and refuses to overwrite an existing output directory. It reproduces the kernel experiment, not a full Terasweep benchmark.

Primary instruction/toolchain references consulted:

- https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/arch/x86_64/fn._mm512_mask_add_pd.html
- https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/arch/x86_64/fn._mm512_cmp_pd_mask.html
- https://blog.rust-lang.org/2025/08/07/Rust-1.89.0/

All performance numbers in this report come from the retained experiment logs, not these external references.

assembly-report.title: Handwritten assembly after intrinsics
assembly-report.text:
# Handwritten AVX-512 after intrinsics: incremental experiment

## The claim this experiment supports

After improving the AVX-512 intrinsics implementation, replacing the **mixed-signal base-scoring kernel** with hand-authored x86-64 assembly increased median scoring throughput by **6.96%** in the principal matched-block experiment. Median accumulated scoring time for 44,560 requested jobs was **54.547 ms with intrinsics** and **50.997 ms with handwritten assembly**: **6.51% less time**, or **1.070× throughput**.

This is a **kernel-level result in a shared VM**, not a Rust Terasweep end-to-end speedup, not an additional 10×, and not a new Limen benchmark. The effect is modest and environment-dependent. We did not multiply it by earlier optimizations measured on another machine.

## What is genuinely handwritten

`src/score8_gpr.S` is a **143-line, manually authored assembly source file**. It was not obtained by compiling C to assembly and relabeling the output. Its calling convention, vector-register assignment, integer-register assignment, masks, branches, numerical instructions, and stores were written explicitly. It is assembled into a separate object and called as an external function.

The function uses eight AVX-512 FP64 lanes for eight independent scoring jobs. The jobs share a fitted model and can have different thresholds and signal rules. Time advances sequentially within every lane.

The final schedule keeps position-state masks in 32-bit general-purpose registers, uses Boolean instructions such as `andn`, and transfers final masks into AVX-512 mask registers for the arithmetic. The accumulators stay in explicitly assigned vector registers. A ternary bitwise instruction applies the same per-lane sign/absolute-value transformation as the tuned intrinsics.

Example from the authored source:

```asm
andn edx, ebx, esi
kmovw k2, edx
vpaddq zmm3{k2}, zmm3, zmm18
vaddpd zmm7{k2}, zmm7, zmm21
vaddpd zmm11{k2}, zmm11, zmm22
```

The file's SHA-256 is:

`7114c244ff89646de1a260a8fcb8654c77f794f5f3a1aa84aeadad37ccc2bfcb`

The code uses separate multiplication and addition. No FMA substitution, FP32 conversion, fast-math, horizontal reassociation, or relaxed correctness tolerance was introduced.

## Why the baseline matters

The objective was an increment **beyond good intrinsics**, not an impressive ratio against scalar code.

The first handwritten version used mask registers for essentially all mask-state arithmetic. It passed validation, but its apparent advantage diminished after improving the intrinsics. That version was not used as evidence of a successful final optimization.

Four prepared-input intrinsics variants were tested: 8-bit ordinary mask expressions and explicit 16-bit mask intrinsics, each compiled with GCC and Clang. The earlier mixed-rule intrinsics implementation was also retained with both compilers. The strongest candidate in discovery was the prepared-input, 8-bit-mask version compiled with Clang 17. It remained faster than the corresponding GCC version in the full-set confirmation.

The final handwritten implementation uses a different hand-scheduled GPR/mask arrangement. The strongest tested intrinsics is not proof that every possible intrinsic implementation has been exhausted. The experiment demonstrates an improvement over the versions actually tested, not the impossibility of expressing equivalent performance in intrinsics.

## Same-wrapper A/B boundary

Both final candidates receive the same `Packed8` input and write the same `Raw8` output. The **same compiled C wrapper** performs grouping, rule/threshold packing, the indirect call, unpacking, and complete output stores. Only the kernel function pointer changes.

Included in the timing:

- grouping the already sorted requested jobs into eight-lane batches;
- packing thresholds, sign/absolute-value transformations, and inclusive-rule masks;
- calling and executing the selected scoring kernel;
- converting its full results into the original 128-byte `Base` representation and storing them.

Excluded:

- file loading, training-statistics preparation, fitting, and prediction;
- sampling, deduplication, constant-signal classification, initial sorting, and chunk planning;
- validation and logging;
- cache management, fee/slippage application, winner selection, and full experiment artifacts.

No trial pruning, new score-cache shortcut, reduced precision, or smaller output contract accounts for the measured assembly increment. The compared variants evaluate identical requested jobs.

## Hardware and toolchain

The execution environment changed from the previously reported AMD host. The current guest reports **Intel Xeon Platinum 8573C**, x86-64 under KVM. Both AVX2 and AVX-512 execute successfully. All results here were remeasured on this guest; the earlier AMD timings were not used as its baseline.

The process is single-threaded and pinned to guest logical CPU 0. The VM exposes five logical CPUs, four CPU-equivalents of quota, and a 4 GiB memory limit. It is shared, not an isolated hardware benchmark.

The common driver is compiled with GCC 14.2.0. The strongest intrinsics object is compiled with Clang 17.0.0. Both use:

```text
-O3 -g -march=x86-64-v3 -ffp-contract=off -fno-fast-math -Wall -Wextra
```

The explicit kernels target AVX-512. The handwritten GPR version also uses BMI1 `andn`; the executable checks the required CPU capabilities. Disassembly and the environment record are retained in the bundle.

## Workload

The uploaded frozen matrices are unchanged: **4,136 training rows, 55 features, and 1,136 test/price rows**. The prior experimental preparation and sampling code is retained. It reconstructs the million-row workload's 2,304 model configurations, 627 failed model configurations, and 648,130 unique valid scoring keys. Of these, **44,560 have mixed signals** and are the timed kernel workload. Eight-lane, same-model/mixed-rule batching has approximately **88.27% useful-lane utilization**.

This is still the inherited C experimental preparation/reference, not a native-x86 build of Rust. No Rust toolchain archive was uploaded in this turn. No production source or executable on the user's Mac was modified.

## Measurements

### Whole-job-set checks

The initial confirmation used 32 rotated repetitions, each timing an uninterrupted evaluation of all 44,560 jobs. The best intrinsics median was **53.928 ms**, versus **50.408 ms** for the final handwritten kernel, a ratio of **1.070×**. Assembly was faster in **22 of 32** same-repetition comparisons.

A subsequent confirmation used the exact shared wrapper, 24 balanced blocks, and four full evaluations per timed block. The strongest intrinsics median per evaluation was **56.301 ms**, versus **52.918 ms** for assembly: **1.064×**. Assembly won **15 of 24** blocks. Large host-related timing excursions remained; no samples were discarded.

### Principal matched-block confirmation

To reduce the exposure of each A/B pair to long timing swings, the sorted jobs were partitioned at **model boundaries**, with up to 16 model groups in a chunk. There were **105 chunks**, and no model was split across chunks. Each chunk was evaluated by both kernels, alternating which ran first by chunk and repetition.

Across 32 complete passes of this protocol:

| Implementation | Median sum of timed chunks per pass | Minimum–maximum |
|---|---:|---:|
| Strongest tested AVX-512 intrinsics | 54.547 ms | 45.527–70.280 ms |
| Handwritten AVX-512 assembly | 50.997 ms | 44.262–66.761 ms |

Ratio of medians: **1.069614×**. Median of per-pass paired ratios: **1.063691×**. Assembly was faster in **27/32 passes**. The reported time is the sum of the timed chunks for one implementation, not the wall duration of the full alternating two-implementation experiment.

The repeated median advantage across these protocols supports a small measured kernel improvement. It is not a general hardware speed guarantee or a claim of tightly bounded statistical uncertainty. Shared-VM noise remains visible, and all outliers are retained.

## Correctness

The final handwritten kernel passed:

| Validation | Result |
|---|---:|
| All unique valid scoring keys from the original million-row sample | 648,130 / 648,130 |
| Complete fields compared for every score | 17, exact integers and FP64 bit patterns |
| Additional thresholds at real predictions, neighboring representable values, signed zero, and observed extrema | 19,440 / 19,440 |
| Prefix lengths, missing-bar control-flow masks, and requested tail-lane counts | 30,240 / 30,240 |
| All timed mixed-signal jobs | 44,560 / 44,560 |

The missing-bar tests change only tradability flags for control-flow coverage, retaining the actual prediction/price arrays. They do not create synthetic market observations and are not included in performance timings. Prefixes include lengths 0, 1, 2, values around vector widths, and the full input; tail tests also detect writes beyond the requested lane count.

The local oracle is the unchanged C reference scorer from the supplied experiment. The prior report separately records that reference matching the original Rust scorer on the Mac for all 648,130 keys. That prior cross-language check is inherited evidence, not a new Rust execution in this session.

## The supported statement

> After the workload reductions and AVX-512 intrinsics optimization, we replaced the remaining mixed-signal scoring kernel with handwritten x86-64 assembly. On the tested Intel Xeon VM, this added approximately 7% median scoring throughput, with bit-for-bit identical complete base-score outputs.

For a **whole-Terasweep** statement, the same two kernels still need to be integrated and timed in the same native Rust runner, with all scheduling, cache, cost, and reporting overhead included. That measurement has not been performed.

## Reproduction

The accompanying archive includes the hand-authored assembly, intrinsics variants, unchanged experimental reference/preparation, frozen inputs, replay script, build commands, raw validation and timing logs, source/input hashes, and disassembly. It excludes generated benchmark binaries and duplicate large output arrays.

Run `./replay.sh /absolute/path/to/a/new/directory` on compatible x86-64 Linux with GCC, Clang, and Python installed. The script refuses to overwrite an existing output directory and verifies the retained source/input checksums before compiling. No network service or additional package download is required.
